name: minikube
summary: A local Kubernetes cluster for developers on Linux, macOS or Windows, in a container, a VM or on the host itself, with laptop-friendly extras.
intro: minikube runs a local cluster inside whatever isolation your machine offers. A driver decides what a “node” is: a container in Docker or Podman, a virtual machine under KVM, Hyper-V, QEMU, VirtualBox, VFkit, Parallels or VMware, an existing machine over SSH, or, with the `none` driver, the host itself. minikube boots that node and sets up Kubernetes with kubeadm, using containerd by default, or CRI-O or Docker. Several clusters live side by side as named profiles, each with its own driver and settings, and `--nodes` adds more nodes on the same machine.

Its stated audience is “application developers and new Kubernetes users”, and it fills the gaps a laptop has compared with a cloud. `minikube tunnel` gives LoadBalancer Services a reachable IP, addons switch on ingress, a registry and other extras with one command, `minikube image build` builds straight into the cluster, and `--kubernetes-version` picks the latest release or any of the six minor versions before it. Where kind is tuned for disposable test clusters in CI, and K3s and MicroK8s also aim at production, minikube’s FAQ says “we strongly discourage using minikube in production”, and by design it listens only on the local network.
strengths: One tool on Linux, macOS and Windows, with a choice of container, VM, SSH or bare-metal drivers
Extras a laptop lacks: `minikube tunnel` for LoadBalancer Services, `minikube service`, filesystem mounts and one-command addons such as ingress and a registry
Runs the latest Kubernetes or one of the six previous minor versions, per cluster, with several clusters as profiles
GPU support (NVIDIA, AMD, Apple) for local AI work, and `minikube pause` or the auto-pause addon to stop Kubernetes eating battery
limits: Explicitly not for production or remote traffic; it is meant to listen only on the local network
Each cluster wants 2 CPUs, 2 GB of free memory and 20 GB of disk, and a VM driver adds a whole guest operating system
Multi-node clusters still run on one host, so they exercise scheduling across nodes, not real hardware failure
Behaviour depends on the driver: Podman is experimental, and on macOS and Windows the Docker driver runs containers inside a VM

source: minikube image build -t my-app:dev .      # built straight into the cluster
minikube tunnel                           # in another terminal: gives it an EXTERNAL-IP
minikube start -p vm-test --driver=qemu   # a second, VM-based cluster

story: In July 2016 Kubernetes had been production-ready for over a year, but, as Google’s Dan Lorenc wrote on the Kubernetes blog, it “has been missing a great local development platform”. Community members set out to build “an easy-to-use, high-fidelity Kubernetes distribution” that would run on Mac, Linux and Windows laptops with a single command. The first release, v0.1.0, came on May 30, 2016 with Linux and macOS binaries, and the official launch accompanied Kubernetes 1.3 that July.

The first design borrowed two pieces. Docker’s libmachine supplied a driver model for creating local VMs (VirtualBox at first, with experimental xhyve and KVM drivers). RedSpread donated localkube, which bundled etcd, DNS, the kubelet and all the control-plane components into one Go binary that ran them as goroutines. minikube later moved to kubeadm, the upstream bootstrapping tool: an experimental kubeadm bootstrapper arrived in v0.22 (September 2017), and localkube was removed in v0.29 (September 2018).

Containers came later. v1.7 (February 2020) added an experimental Docker driver that used kind’s node image, v1.8 promoted it, and the docs now list it as a preferred driver on all three systems. Multi-node clusters arrived as an experiment in v1.9 (March 2020) and lost the experimental label in v1.16 that December.

choices.choice: A driver model for each operating system
choices.why: Reusing Docker’s libmachine gave minikube a ready-made way to create and manage local VMs, so the same cluster could run on Mac, Linux and Windows. The same model later absorbed container, SSH and bare-metal drivers.

localkube made the first cluster a single, quick-to-start process. Switching to kubeadm made minikube set up the official components the way regular clusters do, closer to the original “high-fidelity” goal.

choices.choice: Commands for what a laptop lacks
choices.why: The 2016 launch post noted that LoadBalancers and PersistentVolumes didn’t work out of the box on a local machine. `minikube tunnel`, the bundled storage provisioner and addons now fill those gaps.
